slides.title: The lunch queue peaked during one short window
slides.source: Illustrative dataset for this example. Queue times and operating assumptions are fictional.

blocks.label: What to investigate
blocks.text: The 12:15 group waited longest in the example. A queue alone cannot tell us whether payment, preparation, or pickup caused the delay.

slides.title: Test a separate pickup line at 12:15
slides.source: Illustrative operating proposal. The effect remains unmeasured.

blocks.label: Proposed change
blocks.text: Take preorders for one set meal and hand them out at a marked pickup point. Keep the usual counter open for walk-ins.

blocks.label: Why start here
blocks.text: One time window, one meal and one pickup point give staff a small change they can reverse. Measure both queues so a shorter pickup line cannot hide longer waits elsewhere.

slides.title: Decide after ten comparable lunch periods
slides.source: Illustrative pilot plan. Thresholds are decision criteria, not observed results.

blocks.label: Run the pilot
blocks.text: Use five baseline lunch periods and five pilot periods. The shift lead records queue entry and handoff times.

blocks.label: Protect comparability
blocks.text: Record transactions per period and staffing levels. Flag special events or menu changes before comparing waits.

blocks.label: Decision rule
blocks.text: Expand only if the pickup median falls below eight minutes and the walk-in median stays at or below its own baseline.
